entities.summary:
Borobudur, a monumental Buddhist temple located in Central Java, Indonesia, dates back to the 8th and 9th centuries CE and was constructed during the reign of the Sailendra Dynasty. This site, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991, stands as one of the most significant and largest Buddhist structures in the world, representing the artistic and spiritual zenith of ancient Javanese architecture. Its design incorporates elements of Mahayana Buddhism, and it serves as a pilgrimage site that encapsulates the religious and cultural narratives of Southeast Asia during the Medieval period.

Constructed between 780 and 840 CE, Borobudur features 2,672 relief panels and 504 Buddha statues, showcasing intricate carvings that depict various scenes from the life of the Buddha and Buddhist teachings. The temple's layout is a mandala, symbolizing the cosmos in stone, and it was originally adorned with gilded stupas and vibrant murals. Its rediscovery in the 19th century, after centuries of neglect and overgrowth, prompted significant archaeological and conservation efforts led by figures like Sir Thomas Stamford Raffles, who played a crucial role in bringing the site to global attention and protecting its legacy.

The legacy of Borobudur extends beyond its immediate cultural context; it has influenced modern Buddhist practices and tourism in Indonesia and has become a symbol of national pride, representing the rich historical tapestry of the region. The temple has inspired numerous studies and scholarly works, contributing to our understanding of Southeast Asian history, art, and religion. Furthermore, its architectural style has left a lasting imprint on subsequent temple constructions throughout the region.
